neighbours.label: the change-of-state verb before a spoilage/deterioration outcome: 'go' / 'become' / 'turn' in 'go rancid', 'become stale', 'turn sour'
fire: Keep the nuts in the fridge, because their oils can go rancid in summer heat.
If you leave the bread out uncovered it will quickly become stale.
Milk left on the counter overnight will turn sour by morning.
Store flour in a sealed jar or it may go bad within a few months.
Cut avocados exposed to air soon turn brown and mushy.
Cooking oil kept near the stove tends to become rancid faster.
Opened wine will go off after a few days unless you cork it.
Without refrigeration, fresh fish can spoil and become unsafe to eat.
quiet: Keep the nuts in the fridge, because we can go shopping again in summer.
If you leave the bread out uncovered the children will quickly eat it.
Milk left on the counter overnight should be turned into pancakes by morning.
Store flour in a sealed jar so you can go baking whenever you like.
Cut avocados in half and turn them over onto the board.
Cooking oil kept near the stove tends to become easier to reach.
Opened wine will go well with dinner if you pour it now.
Without refrigeration, fresh fish should be cooked and eaten the same day.

notes: Card: peaks on ' go' ('can go rancid'), ' become' ('become rancid'), ' turn' ('turn dark'), ' was' ('food that was too old'); the - pole's logit effect promotes spoiled/stale/bad/contaminated/old, so it predicts the spoilage word. Near misses use the same verbs in non-spoilage senses.
